aspectTitle: False logotype / branding exemption — informational text dressed up as a brand mark
aspectDescription: TT step 1a and the Understanding 'A logo containing text' example exempt logotypes ('text that is part of a logo or brand name') from 1.4.5 because 'the visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo.' The genuinely hard, human-only judgment is distinguishing a real wordmark/brand identity from ordinary informational text (a tagline, marketing slogan, navigation label, deadline notice, or paragraph of prose) that an author has merely set in a nice typeface, exported as an image, and parked in a header or wrapped in class='logo' to dodge the SC. A one-word company word
scenario: Fintech masthead 'brand lockup': a genuine one-word wordmark image ('Northwind', exempt logotype) stacked directly above a second image whose pixels spell the full marketing tagline 'Northwind — the smartest way to manage your money, every day', styled to read as part of the logo. Same branding zone, opposite verdicts; the tagline is ordinary marketing prose that must be live text.
mechanism: The tagline's words are SVG <text> glyphs in an inline-SVG data: URI (verified: string absent from document.body.innerText; rasterises at 200% zoom). A low-vision user cannot resize/recolour the sentence because it is pixels, not text. The wordmark image shares that limitation but is PERMITTED under the logotype exemption; the tagline is NOT, because the same information is expressible as styled live text with the author's technologies, so text must be used (1.4.5).
primarySelector: header.masthead img.tagline-banner[alt="Northwind — the smartest way to manage your money, every day"]

A one-word company word
scenario: SaaS pricing page where the real brand name 'Quanta' is live text, but the pricing section's heading 'Our 2026 Pricing Plans' is rendered as a flat image and wrapped in <div class="logo" role="img" aria-label="Our 2026 Pricing Plans">, set in the brand display face, argued to be 'branding'. A styled section heading is WCAG's canonical image-of-text example, not a logo.
mechanism: The heading exists only as SVG glyphs inside an wrapped by role="img". The role=img has an accessible name via aria-label so a screen reader hears the words, but 1.4.5 concerns visual customisation: a low-vision user who needs the title at 200% in their own colours gets a blurred raster instead of reflowed, recoloured text. The logotype/branding exemption applies only when presentation is essential to a brand identity; a section heading's information is fully expressible as live CSS text, so text must be used.

A screen-reader user still hears the link names from the hidden spans, but 1.4.5 protects the visual customisation a low-vision sighted user needs, which is denied. Navigation labels are not a logotype; their information is fully expressible as live CSS text.

The deadline notice is styled to sit inside the official lockup, with alt equal to its visible text so a captioned-image heuristic is fooled.

The crest legitimately invokes the exemption.

aspectTitle: Customizability exception — image of text adjustable (or fake-adjustable) via on-page controls (C30)
aspectDescription: The SC text itself passes images of text 'where a particular presentation of text is essential or can be visually customized,' and TT Test 7.E condition 2 passes an image of text if it 'can be visually customized: adjust the font, size, color, and background with controls provided by the web page.' Technique C30 (CSS image-replacement with a switch control) and the Understanding 'Dynamically Generated Images' / 'Customizable font settings' examples are the canonical PASS-by-customization route. Evaluating this requires a human to find the controls, operate them, and judge whether activating th
scenario: E-commerce fashion site with a third-party 'accessibility' A-/A/A+ font-scaler toolbar. The campaign headline 'The Spring Linen Edit' is an inline-SVG image of text. The toolbar genuinely resizes the live HTML body copy (via a CSS --fs custom property) but has zero effect on the SVG headline, so the one image of text on the page cannot be customized despite a working customization control.
mechanism: Image of text (inline SVG <text>) sized in absolute SVG user units; the customization control only multiplies a CSS custom property consumed by .scalable HTML text, so activating A+ enlarges paragraphs but never the headline. Customizability exception (TT 7.E condition 2 / C30) not met for the image of text itself. Verified headless: SVG width unchanged after A+ while lede font-size grew (--fs 1->1.3).

In the poster corner is an 'Adjust poster appearance' toolbar with A-/A+ and three colour swatches, styled and role-marked exactly like a working C30 control. Activating any control re-renders nothing, so the customizability exception is faked. Verified headless: scriptCount=0, controls are SPAN tag, poster geometry unchanged after click.

scenario: Higher-ed credential-verification page renders its 'Certificate of Completion' heading into a <canvas> (a genuine image of text). A real C30 customization control (A-/A+ size + a colour <select> incl. a high-contrast black) sits BEFORE the image and truly re-renders the canvas glyphs at the chosen size and colour — it redraws (not CSS-scale), so the text stays sharp at every size with no pixelation and the full wording is always drawn. The canonical PASS-by-customization boundary, confirmable only by operating the control.
mechanism: Canvas image of text re-rasterized on demand: each A+/colour change recomputes canvas dimensions and calls fillText at the new font size/colour (DPR-aware), so output is sharp (no pixelation, satisfying TT note 2a) and complete (same string), with aria-label kept in sync. Control located near the start of the page per C30. Verified headless: canvas.width changed on A+, sizeOut 36px->50px, colour select applied.

scenario: Family-trattoria recipe page presents Nonna's entire ragù recipe (title, 'Serves 6', full ingredient list, numbered method) as a single inline-SVG image of text. A 'Customize reading appearance' panel offers three theme buttons (Cream/Parchment/Mint). Pressing them genuinely changes the PAGE background colour — so the controls feel alive — but the recipe SVG is never re-rendered, recoloured, resized, or swapped. Superficially customizable, substantively not: the customization targets the chrome around the image, not the image of text.

Customization must adjust the image of text's font/size/colour/background (TT 7.E condition 2); recolouring the page behind a fixed bitmap does not. Verified headless: body background changed cream->mint while recipe SVG width unchanged.

scenario: Newspaper 'Quote of the Day' pull-quote delivered as a dynamically generated image of text — a 150x52 low-resolution PNG raster of an italic quote. A 'Display size' <select> (Small/Medium/Large/Extra large) re-requests the image at a larger size (the canonical dynamic-image customization). The control works and the card grows, but the quote engine has only the one low-res master raster, so larger sizes are the same pixels upscaled and the text turns blurry/blocky — a borderline FAIL on the no-pixelation sub-requirement.
mechanism: source is a true 150x52 PNG bitmap (naturalWidth 150) with image-rendering: pixelated; the size selector re-assigns the same master src and grows display width (e.g. to 660px, ~4.4x), so the glyphs pixelate rather than re-render sharp. Fails TT 7.E note 2a (size customization must be without pixelation). Verified headless: PNG decodes (150x52), upscales to 660px display, image-rendering computed 'pixelated'; screenshots show crisp Small vs blocky/blurry Extra large.

scenario: Auto-insurance quote summary renders its legally required 'Important disclosures' block as an SVG image of text. A real C30-style control (A-/A+ size + High contrast colour) genuinely re-renders the disclosure as fresh sharp SVG text at the chosen size/colour. The trap: the re-render template silently OMITS the third line — the 14-day cooling-off / cancellation right present in the default image. The controls work; the customized output is functional yet not equivalent, and the loss lands precisely on the user who must customize to read it.
mechanism: Default SVG markup contains four disclosure lines incl. the cooling-off clause; the JS re-render path rebuilds the SVG from a LINES array that has only three lines (cooling-off dropped). On first interaction the handler replaces #discWrap's SVG with the non-equivalent version. 1.4.5 customizability requires the customized image keep 'the same effect and information' (TT 7.E). Verified headless: default 4 lines with cooling-off present; after A+ -> 3 lines, cooling-off absent.

aspectDescription: The images-of-text definition note excludes 'text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content,' citing 'graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text' (TT adds CAPTCHA). The detection step is explicitly OCR-like: the tester must FIRST decide whether an image that contains text is fundamentally a graph/screenshot/diagram/infographic (out of scope, INAPPLICABLE) or is an image-of-text dressed up (in scope, potentially FAIL). scenario: Marketing weekly digest with two flat images side by side: a GENUINE bar chart (bar heights encode the data, words are axis labels — excluded graph) next to a 'Paid campaign breakdown' that wears chart chrome (teal title strip, legend swatch, gridlines, coloured cells) but has ZERO graphical encoding — every spend rectangle is identical width, so all data lives in text laid out in a grid. The right image is a table-as-picture, i.e. an image of text.
mechanism: The right image (#fake-chart) presents tabular data AS an image RATHER THAN as text: dollar values pixelate on zoom, cannot be recoloured/reflowed/selected, and a screen reader gets one alt string instead of a navigable table. None of its visual content (chips, gridlines, legend) conveys meaning beyond the words, so the 1.4.5 'significant other visual content' exclusion does not apply — unlike the left chart whose bar heights genuinely carry the data.

The flourishes make it FEEL like a picture with significant other visual content, but the ornament carries no information — courses, dish names, prices, the soup of the day, and the allergen note are entirely text laid out decoratively. scenario: An HR portal publishes a reimbursement 'Approval flow' as one image, titled 'Approval flow' and captioned 'Approval flowchart' to invite the 1.4.5 diagrams exclusion. But the picture has NO boxes, arrows, connectors, decision diamonds, or branching — it is five numbered sentences stacked on alternating tinted bands. The only structure is top-to-bottom order, which a plain ordered list already provides. It is an image of an ordered list of steps.

Because the picture contains no boxes/arrows/branches, none of its visual content is 'significant' — it is an ordered list in disguise, squarely in scope of 1.4.5 (a real flowchart with decision branches would be excluded).

scenario: A municipal permits portal gates an application behind a 'Verify it's you' step that looks like a CAPTCHA (code image, refresh button, input, audio link). Trusted Tester excludes CAPTCHA from images of text — but only because a real CAPTCHA's distortion/noise IS the security function and cannot be reproduced as live text. This image renders the clean word 'SUNFLOWER' in a serif display font on a flat panel: no warping, no per-glyph rotation, no overlapping strokes, no noise, no occluding lines. It is ordinary styled text saved as a picture.
mechanism: A real CAPTCHA's distortion legitimately cannot be replaced by live text (why it is excluded). This clean image's word could be presented as text (or replaced by a genuine accessible challenge) with no loss, so the exclusion fails and 1.4.5 applies: text is presented AS an image RATHER THAN as text, with no way for a low-vision user to enlarge/recolour it without pixelation. Clean styled text is not the 'significant other visual content' (distortion/noise) that defines a CAPTCHA.

scenario: An insurance broker presents three plan tiers (Essential / Plus / Premier) as a single comparison image with a 'Most popular' ribbon, green check and grey cross glyphs in the coverage rows, and column dividers. The icons/ribbon tempt the 1.4.5 exclusion, but they are redundant: each check/cross marks a yes/no fact already printed as a word, and the ribbon repeats 'Most popular,' also printed. Plan names, prices, deductibles, coverage limits and the yes/no facts are all text in a grid — a comparison table rendered as an image. Tightest borderline in the set.
mechanism: The comparison is presented AS an image RATHER THAN as text: prices/deductibles pixelate on enlargement, cannot be recoloured, and a wide table cannot reflow on mobile (the image overflows); a screen reader gets one alt string instead of a navigable table with row/column headers. Because the check/cross icons and ribbon convey nothing beyond the words, the non-text content is not 'significant' and the exclusion does not apply (a true coverage heatmap encoding values in colour intensity would be excluded).

aspectTitle: 'In addition to' MET condition — image of text accompanied by the same content as visible live text
aspectDescription: The Understanding note: the SC 'is intended to address situations where images of text are used rather than text. Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.' The 'event poster + CMS text' example is the canonical PASS: the poster image would fail alone, but because the SAME text is ALSO posted as live, visible text next to it, 1.4.5 is satisfied. The hard human judgment is verifying EQUIVALENCE (same information, not a partial summary) AND VISIBILITY (genuinely presented to the user
scenario: Community-arts events calendar: a folk-festival poster (image of text) with the FULL poster contents — date, doors/music times, venue + address, three-act line-up, ticket price, booking URL — reproduced verbatim as visible, restyleable live HTML (a <dl> + <ul>) directly beneath it. The canonical 'in addition to' PASS the ACT corpus lacks.
mechanism: The poster's words exist twice: once as immutable image pixels (inline-SVG data: URI) and once as live HTML. A low-vision user can zoom/recolour the live <dl>/<ul>; a screen-reader user hears the full programme from it. Because the SAME information is presented BOTH as the image AND as adjustable live text, the Understanding-note 'in addition to text … both presented to the user' met-condition is satisfied and 1.4.5 is met even though the image alone would fail.

aspectTitle: 'In addition to' MET condition — image of text accompanied by the same content as visible live text
aspectDescription: The Understanding note: the SC 'is intended to address situations where images of text are used rather than text. Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.' The 'event poster + CMS text' example is the canonical PASS: the poster image would fail alone, but because the SAME text is ALSO posted as live, visible text next to it, 1.4.5 is satisfied. The hard human judgment is verifying EQUIVALENCE (same information, not a partial summary) AND VISIBILITY (genuinely presented to the user
scenario: Live-music venue gig listing: a poster image of text states the headline act, tour, date (Fri 7 Nov 2026), doors 7:30, two support acts, 18+ policy, and £24.50 price; the adjacent live text reproduces only the act + tour name in the <h1>, a marketing blurb, and three generic 'tag' chips. Text exists 'in addition to' the image but omits the date, doors, supports, age policy, and price.
mechanism: A blind or low-vision user gets, as live text, only the act/tour name + blurb + tags; the date, doors time, both support acts, the 18+ restriction, and the £24.50 price live ONLY as pixels in the poster (whose alt is just a label). Because the accompanying live text does not convey the SAME information as the image, the 'in addition to' met-condition does not rescue those facts and 1.4.5 fails for them.

aspectTitle: 'In addition to' MET condition — image of text accompanied by the same content as visible live text
aspectDescription: The Understanding note: the SC 'is intended to address situations where images of text are used rather than text. Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.' The 'event poster + CMS text' example is the canonical PASS: the poster image would fail alone, but because the SAME text is ALSO posted as live, visible text next to it, 1.4.5 is satisfied. The hard human judgment is verifying EQUIVALENCE (same information, not a partial summary) AND VISIBILITY (genuinely presented to the user
scenario: Interior-architecture studio testimonial: a designed quote-card image of text, paired in the DOM with a live <blockquote> containing word-for-word identical wording 'in addition to' the image — but the <blockquote> carries the studio's reusable visually-hidden (sr-only 1px clip-path:inset(50%)) helper, so it is removed from the visible page. Equivalence is perfect; visibility is broken.
mechanism: A screen-reader user does hear the full quote from the clipped <blockquote>, but 1.4.5 protects people who can SEE text yet need to restyle it. For a low-vision user who needs the quote at 200% in high contrast, the only thing on screen is the immutable image; the equivalent text is clipped to a 1px offscreen box and cannot be enlarged, recoloured, or reflowed. The note requires BOTH the image and the text be 'presented to the user'; hidden text is exposed to AT but not visibly presented, so the met-condition does not apply.

scenario: Café daily-specials: a photographed chalkboard image of text shows TODAY's specials (Spiced Parsnip Soup £6.50 / Wild Mushroom Risotto £12.50 / Sticky Toffee Pudding £6.00); the live 'Text version' <ul> beneath it was not refreshed this week and still lists LAST week's specials and prices (Carrot & Coriander Soup £6.00 / Beef Lasagne £11.95 / Lemon Cheesecake £5.50). The 'in addition to' met-condition requires the accompanying text to convey the SAME information as the image; stale text conveys DIFFERENT information, so the condition is not satisfied and 1.4.5 is not met.

scenario: District-council garden-waste notice: the entire substantive notice (collection day change, £45 subscription, 20 June deadline, 'will not be emptied' warning, renewal URL/phone) is a single image of text with a faithful, complete alt attribute; there is NO visible live-text version of the notice anywhere on the page. But 1.4.5 protects users who can SEE text yet need to change how it looks; for them the alt is invisible — exposed only to AT, never rendered, so it cannot be enlarged, recoloured, or reflowed on screen. scenario: Residential-building water-shutoff notice: a single bilingual flyer image of text contains both an ENGLISH block and an ESPAÑOL block carrying the same shutoff details; the resident portal renders a live 'Text version' 'in addition to' the image, but a volunteer transcribed only the English half. aspectTitle: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspectDescription: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting
scenario: A typography magazine feature 'Why Garamond still wins for long reads' bakes its own ordinary body paragraphs (history + argument + recommendation) into a single Garamond image 'so you can see the typeface in real use'. The article ABOUT a font is treated as if it were a font specimen, abusing the 'Representation of a font family' exception. A genuine live-text letterform specimen ('Hh Aa Gg Qq') sits above it for contrast; only the running prose was wrongly imaged.
mechanism: The article's running prose exists only as SVG <text> glyphs inside an inline-SVG data: URI image (verified: 'Claude Garamont cut his romans' absent from live innerText, present in alt). The words are ordinary information, not a demonstration of letterforms, so re-typesetting in the user's own font would lose nothing essential. A user needing a larger/dyslexia-friendly/high-contrast font, wider spacing, or reflow at 200-400% zoom cannot adjust this fixed raster and it pixelates on enlargement. The font-representation exception does not apply because the text is the content, not a specimen.

aspectTitle: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspectDescription: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting
scenario: A type foundry's retail specimen page for a new display typeface ('Brume Display') the visitor does not have installed and that is not licensed for web embedding. Specimen images show the actual letterforms ('Velvet Morning', ffi/ffl ligatures, swash Q R K) because the appearance of the glyphs IS what is being sold; re-typesetting in a fallback font would show a different typeface and defeat the representation. The page also provides the same strings as live, selectable, resizable fallback-font text and an editable size-adjustable preview. PASS twin to case-01.
mechanism: The specimen images legitimately use the font-representation exception: substituting the font would defeat the purpose of the representation, so the image of text cannot be replaced by text with the same effect. The page does NOT strand users needing adjustable text — each specimen string also appears as live HTML (verified: 'Velvet Morning' present in BOTH image and live innerText), and an editable preview with a working font-size slider (drives --preview-size) lets low-vision users enlarge/recolour the live copy. This is the conformant 'in addition to' + customizable pattern.

aspectTitle: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspectDescription: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting
scenario: A museum 'Plan your visit' page renders its modern 2024 opening hours and a donation appeal as a faux-antique parchment image — torn-edge border, sepia, cursive quill font — 'to give the page a historic feel'. There is no original artefact: the text was authored today, so its original format is HTML, not a period letter. The 'representation of a letter / original-format-essential' exception is abused to justify avoidable images of text. FAIL twin to case-06.
mechanism: The opening hours, season, and suggested donation exist only as SVG <text> glyphs in an inline-SVG data: URI styled as parchment (verified: 'Harrowby Hall is open Wednesday' absent from live innerText, present in alt). Because the text was authored today and its appearance conveys nothing about a historical time period, the visual presentation is not essential — live HTML would convey the same effect while remaining adjustable. The decorative cursive font additionally harms low-vision/cognitive legibility and the raster pixelates at 200-400% zoom, with no way to resize, recolour, or reflow.

aspectTitle: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspectDescription: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting
scenario: A webmail compose toolbar replaces the symbolic glyphs (B/I/ABC) with images of the FULL WORD LABELS 'Bold', 'Italic', 'Underline', 'Spell check' because single letters were deemed 'too cryptic'. Those are English words — a sequence that expresses something in human language — so the symbolic-text-characters exception does not apply; they are ordinary label text rendered as images and should be live text. Each button also carries a matching aria-label, so AT names are correct.
mechanism: The button labels are human-language words that exist only as SVG <text> glyphs inside images (verified: 'Spell check' absent from live innerText, present via aria-label). The accessible name comes from aria-label so braille/screen-reader output is fine (1.1.1/4.1.2 met), but a sighted low-vision user relying on OS/browser font scaling, a dyslexia-friendly typeface, or forced-colors mode cannot adjust these labels — they are fixed pixels that blur on zoom and won't recolour. Because the words express human language they are not symbolic characters, so live text could and should convey the same effect.

aspectTitle: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspectDescription: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting
scenario: A cloud-storage Terms-of-Service page renders its binding clauses (governing law, liability cap, arbitration / class-action waiver) as a single image and labels it 'a type sample of our house legal typeface, Pinevault Text' via both a figcaption and an aria-describedby note. It is not a specimen — it is legally operative contract text the user must read, resize, and reflow. A human reviewer must reject the bogus 'type sample' essential-presentation justification.
mechanism: The operative legal text exists only as SVG <text> glyphs inside an inline-SVG data: URI (verified: 'binding individual arbitration' absent from live innerText, present in alt). A low-vision user needing 200-400% zoom cannot enlarge the arbitration clause without pixelation; a forced-colors user cannot recolour it; reflow to a single column is impossible for a fixed raster. The information is the words of a binding contract, not a demonstration of letterforms, so the visual presentation is not essential and live HTML would convey the same effect. The self-applied 'type sample' label does not change what the content is.

aspectTitle: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspectDescription: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting
scenario: A museum object page presents a scanned 11th-century Chinese seal-script hanging scroll (山高水長). The artefact IS the brushwork — stroke order, ink density, and the individual calligrapher's hand — so re-typesetting in a modern seal font would show a different object and lose the historical information. The genuine original-format-essential exception. The page also provides the modern Unicode transcription (lang=zh-Hant), romanisation, and English translation beside it as live, selectable, resizable text. PASS twin to case-03.
mechanism: The scroll image's accessible name transcribes the four characters AND describes the calligraphic form (rounded even-weight strokes, the lean of 長, dry-brush flecking on 水 — verified image-side only), so AT users learn both the words and what is visually significant. The irreplaceable information (this hand's brushwork) is what the image preserves, so the image of text is essential and permitted. The page also provides live selectable resizable HTML (zh-Hant transcription + romanisation + translation), so low-vision users can enlarge/recolour adjustable text while researchers get the original form.

aspectTitle: Core image-of-text-vs-live-text detection across delivery mechanisms and decoy live text
aspectDescription: The SC's foundational requirement — 'If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text' — depends on a human first recognizing that an image actually contains rendered text (OCR-like detection) and then confirming the same visual effect was achievable in HTML/CSS so the content should have been live text. The hard cases require semantic judgment: text baked into a CSS background-image or pseudo-element (no , no alt, invisible to most checkers), text rendered via SVG inside an image vs. live selectable S
scenario: Aurelia Trust bank masthead: the site-name wordmark is an inline-SVG (image of text) delivered via CSS background-image on the <h1>, whose only real DOM text is a visually-hidden sr-only decoy span saying the same words; an identical-looking live-text twin (Aurelia Savings) proves the look was achievable.
mechanism:
Image of text delivered as a CSS background-image (no /alt) on an

; visible serif wordmark is SVG inside the background, absent from DOM/accessibility tree and non-resizable/non-recolorable, while an sr-only span provides programmatic text. Visual presentation is plainly achievable as live text (the twin heading), no logotype/essential exception applies.

aspectDescription: The SC's foundational requirement — 'If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text' — depends on a human first recognizing that an image actually contains rendered text (OCR-like detection) and then confirming the same visual effect was achievable in HTML/CSS so the content should have been live text. scenario: Lakeshore Public Library reading room: the featured excerpt (opening of The Little Prince) is a genuine raster PNG of a six-line body paragraph embedded in <svg role=img><image href=data:image/png> with a decoy <title>/<desc> naming the book; a sibling block renders Whitman as live, selectable SVG <text> as the PASS/inapplicable foil.
mechanism: A multi-line paragraph of body prose is shipped as a raster PNG inside an SVG <image>, given an accessible name by decoy <title>/<desc>; the prose is fixed pixels (non-resizable, non-recolorable, pixelates on zoom; an 'A+ Larger text' control visibly fails). The same serif body look is achievable with @font-face/live text, proven by the adjacent live SVG <text> block; no essential exception applies to a novel's paragraph.

scenario: Trattoria del Ponte dinner menu: each dish name is painted from a single SVG sprite-sheet set as a CSS background-image and revealed per row with background-position (brush-script 'calligraphy'); the row's real text node is pushed off-screen and a generic aria-label='menu item' sits on each <li>; prices are live text.
mechanism: Dish names are images of text delivered as a CSS sprite-sheet background (no /alt), clipped per row; the placeholder text node is indented off-screen and a generic aria-label supplies the row name. The brush-script presentation is achievable with a licensed @font-face webfont and live text; the names are words (not a picture with other significant visual content), are not a logotype, and are not user-customizable.

scenario: The Meridian Review long-form article: the large italic pull-quote ('We stopped designing streets for cars...') is painted by a CSS ::before pseudo-element whose content box carries a background-image SVG of the quote glyphs; the quote words exist nowhere in the DOM, only a live <figcaption> attribution does. This is the WCAG 'A quote' example built as an image of text.
mechanism:
The pull-quote is an image of text delivered through a ::before generated-content background-image — no , no alt, and the quotation words are entirely absent from the DOM and accessibility tree. Generated-content background images ignore font-size/color/forced-colors and pixelate on zoom. The italic/indented/large-serif effect is the textbook achievable-in-CSS case (live
+ CSS); not essential, not customizable.

scenario:
Birchwood Outfitters storefront: the 'Summer Clearance Event' category heading is a real raster PNG wrapped in an

, with a perfect descriptive decoy alt ('Summer Clearance Event'); a live-text heading 'New Arrivals for Fall' shows the achievable treatment. A descriptive alt satisfies 1.1.1 but does not satisfy 1.4.5.
mechanism: A styled heading is delivered as a non-resizable raster bitmap image of text; the alt is an exact transcription so 1.1.1 and naive heading checks are satisfied, but the displayed heading pixelates on zoom and ignores user font/color/forced-colors settings. The bold red look is trivially achievable with live HTML+CSS (demonstrated by the adjacent live heading); not a logotype, not essential, not customizable — so it fails 1.4.5 despite correct alt.

aspectDescription: The SC's foundational requirement — 'If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text' — depends on a human first recognizing that an image actually contains rendered text (OCR-like detection) and then confirming the same visual effect was achievable in HTML/CSS so the content should have been live text. The hard cases require semantic judgment: text baked into a CSS background-image or pseudo-element (no , no alt, invisible to most checkers), text rendered via SVG inside an image vs. live selectable S
scenario: Halcyon Type Foundry product page for the typeface 'Meridian Display': the large character-set specimen is a raster PNG showing the actual letterforms of the font being sold (with a descriptive alt), surrounded by live-text price, feature list, buy button, and preview field. The achievability/essential gate makes this a deliberate PASS boundary foil.
mechanism: The specimen is an image of text, but its visual presentation IS the information (the exact glyphs of this specific typeface); rendering it as substitutable live text would defeat the representation, so 1.4.5's essential/not-achievable exception applies. A text alternative satisfies 1.1.1, and all surrounding UI is live text — so the page passes for the right reason.
